extracted.intended_audience: students and authors preparing mathematics papers (undergraduate/graduate/early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, well-formatted mathematical papers: notation, equations, proofs, typography, structure, and proofreading aimed at authors preparing math manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow good writing habits
rubrics_metrics.description: A math paper should be punctuated, spelled, and organized clearly, like papers in other disciplines; math paragraphs are usually shorter and very long paragraphs should be split when they contain more than one main idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General guidance to ensure readability: check punctuation, spelling, and organization; break long paragraphs into separate ones when multiple ideas appear. (Example: very long paragraph likely contains more than one main idea.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Never begin a sentence with a symbol or number
rubrics_metrics.description: Never begin a sentence with a symbol or a number; always start with a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: starting a sentence 'n = 2m for some m...' instead of 'Thus n = 2m for some m...' (Exceptions for spoken language do not apply to writing.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer words when symbols are not part of same expression
rubrics_metrics.description: If two symbols are not part of the same mathematical expression, they should not appear adjacent without intervening words or punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'If n=0 n^2>0.' Good: 'If n=0, n^2>0.' or 'If n=0 then n^2>0.' Use commas or words to separate distinct mathematical items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose natural variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing a new variable, use one which looks natural in that context (common sense choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bad: 'Let m be a prime.' Good: 'Let p be a prime.' Bad: 'Pick an element of X, say t.' Good: '...say x.' For multiple elements prefer x and y or x_1 and x_2 rather than confusing letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always define new notation and its logical standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Always define new notation (is it a number? a function? of what type?) and be clear about its logical standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very bad: 'Since n is composite, n = ab.' Better: 'Since n is composite, n = ab for some integers a and b greater than 1.' Specify domains, quantification, and constraints so the notation conveys content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give multiple meanings to the same variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reuse a variable name for different objects within a proof or argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Using 'm' for both factors a=2m and b=2m. Correct: use distinct placeholders (a=2m, b=2n) so the logic is valid and not misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading meaning into notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not cram multiple pieces of information into a single notation token; be explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Let x>0 ∈ Z.' Good: 'Let x be an integer, with x>0.' or 'Let x be a positive integer.' Avoid ambiguous combined notations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write out logical quantifiers and connectives in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using symbols like ∀, ∃, ∧, ∨ in ordinary mathematical writing except in logic papers; write out 'for all', 'there exists', 'and', 'or' in ordinary language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'If ∃ a root then...' Good: 'If there is a root then...' Use natural language to improve readability for broad audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blackboard abbreviations and silly abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid abbreviations used on the blackboard (WLOG, s.t., iff) and other informal shortcuts in formal writing; write the phrase fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'WLOG, we can assume...' Good: 'Without loss of generality, we can assume...' Bad: 'x s.t. f(x)>0' Good: 'x such that f(x)>0.' Use standard full forms in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use superfluous notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a piece of notation is unnecessary in your writing, omit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Every differentiable function f is continuous.' Good: 'Every differentiable function is continuous.' Avoid introducing symbols that are never used or add no content (e.g., naming a matrix when not referred to again).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish equations from expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation contains an equals sign; an expression does not. Do not call expressions equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '(a^3 + b^3)^2' is an expression, not an equation. Use correct terminology to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important equations on their own line to emphasize significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Place key formulae or conclusions as displayed, centered equations on their own line to make them more visible and easier to absorb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both inline and displayed are acceptable, but display signals importance. Example: display Pythagorean theorem or parametric formula; continue the sentence after the displayed formula on a new line as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number only equations that will be referenced later
rubrics_metrics.description: Equations that will be referred to later should have an equation number placed to the left to serve as a reference label; unreferenced equations need not be labelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbering judiciously. Example: label (3.1) for later citation; omit numbers for one-off displayed identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format multi-step computations with successive displayed lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting the steps of a computation with several steps, display them on successive lines and avoid repeating an unchanged left side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: putting entire computation on one line or repeating left side multiple times. Good: show the left-hand side once and then successive equalities indented under it for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed equations as part of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Equations and expressions are part of a sentence and should be punctuated accordingly: period if it ends the sentence, comma if the sentence continues, or no punctuation when natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: End-of-sentence displayed equation should have a period; mid-sentence display should have a comma if a natural pause occurs. Ensure surrounding prose and punctuation make a grammatical sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pointless parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include unnecessary parentheses in mathematical expressions when they add no information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: '(x+y)(x−y) = (x^2−y^2)' — the right parentheses are pointless. Remove redundant parentheses for cleaner expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parentheses to disambiguate subtraction vs negative sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parentheses to prevent ambiguous meaning between subtraction and multiplication by a negative number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very bad: '(a+b) − c = −ac − bc' (ambiguous). Good: '(a+b)(−c) = −ac − bc.' Insert parentheses where needed to show intended grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas correctly; avoid badly placed commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas indicate brief pauses and should not be used where no pause belongs; incorrect commas can break sentence flow or indicate sentence boundary errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'The condition we want is, a = 2b.' Good: 'The condition we want is a = 2b.' Use full stops when appropriate rather than commas that create run-ons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Let..., then...' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not chain 'Let ..., then ...' with a comma; write separate sentences or use 'so' to link cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Let n be an even number, then n=2m for some m∈Z.' Good: 'Let n be an even number. Then n=2m for some m∈Z.' Or '...so n=2m...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting sentences with 'Which' incorrectly
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences beginning with 'Which' are usually fragments; integrate the clause into the preceding sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'The sequence tends to 1. Which means xn>0 for large n.' Good: 'The sequence tends to 1, which means xn>0 for large n.' Make relative clauses part of the prior sentence or rephrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader where you are going (use signposting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state proof strategies or the plan of attack (e.g., 'We will prove this by induction on n' or 'We argue by contradiction').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear signposting phrases to orient the reader: 'We will prove...', 'Now we consider...', 'To see why...'. These phrases help follow the structure of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use key logical words to show reasoning and vary wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words like since, because, on the other hand, observe, note to show reasoning flow; vary word choice to avoid monotony and consider rewriting paragraphs to improve flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive short sentences that mechanically apply previous results; instead combine and restructure to expose the reasoning clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch spelling and usage (careful with its/it's etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread spelling and word usage; be aware of differences in varieties of English and do not let native-language grammar mislead English mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Use 'it's' only for 'it is' and 'its' for possession. Check confusing pairs (necessary/neccessary, discriminate/discriminant). Non-native speakers should verify grammatical constructions that differ from their native languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize single-letter mathematical variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Single letters used as variables, parameters, or function names are typed in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: non-italic single-letter variables or italicized numbers. Examples: a x^2 + bx + c — letters italic; ensure derivatives and function names follow typographic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers are never typed in italics; italic numbers look bad and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: putting italics around numerals in formulas. Keep numerals upright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize multi-letter function names
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional function names involving several letters (sin, cos, log) should not be set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'sin θ' in italics. Good: 'sin θ' in upright font. Likewise 'log ab = log a + log b' — function names upright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize (or emphasize) new defined terms on first occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a new term for the first time, emphasize it (commonly in italics; some books use bold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: Put newly defined term in italics on first appearance to signal definition. Do not label theorems as definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theorem/lemma/corollary labels appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem is a main result; a lemma is primarily a result used to prove a theorem; a corollary follows from a theorem. Their naming signals the author's view of relative importance and the usual ordering (lemma before theorem, corollary after theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not have strings of lemmas that don't lead to a theorem; avoid mislabeling (e.g., don't call a theorem a definition). Historical exceptions exist where important results remain called lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are not theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition states terminology and is not a theorem; do not label a proposition that requires proof as a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: calling the derivative-additivity result a 'definition' when it requires proof. Ensure definitions introduce terms and theorems state provable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Latin abbreviations correctly (i.e., e.g., etc., et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use i.e., e.g., etc., et al. with their correct meanings; in American English place a comma after these abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i.e. = 'that is' (use to clarify), e.g. = 'for example' (use for examples), etc. = 'and other things', et al. = 'and other people'. Examples show misuse and correct placements; prefer 'i.e.,' for clarifying lists of specific items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread thoroughly before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread your paper (draft or final) from the perspective of the target audience; ensure clarity, correctness, examples, and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist: (1) Do the ideas flow logically? (2) Is there proper motivation? (3) Are there suitable examples/counterexamples? (4) Does the math make sense — no logical/computational errors; give complete reasoning and finish proofs? (5) Is it written correctly — grammar, spelling, punctuation, references (correct theorem numbers), and consistent notation?
